title: Brainstem Atlas
subtitle: Trace midbrain, pons, medulla, nuclei and ascending systems
altText: Interactive chalkboard-style anatomical atlas of Brainstem with labelled regions and pathway relationships.
learningObjectives: Locate major cranial-nerve and arousal systems.
Recognise clinically urgent patterns associated with brainstem dysfunction.

sections.explainSimply: The brainstem links the brain, spinal cord and cerebellum while regulating breathing, heart rate, sleep, arousal and many cranial-nerve functions.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Brainstem systems shape state regulation, sensory gating and autonomic stability, meaning small lesions can produce broad cognitive, behavioural and medical effects.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: The midbrain, pons and medulla contain cranial-nerve nuclei, reticular formation, long ascending and descending tracts, neuromodulatory nuclei and cardiorespiratory centres. Compact anatomy makes focal lesions clinically dense and often crossed in their signs.
sections.thinkOfItLike: It is a compact transport hub and life-support control room: major routes pass through while local stations regulate essential functions.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Changes in arousal, eye movements, swallowing, autonomic regulation or crossed sensory-motor signs can indicate urgent brainstem pathology.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Attributing fluctuating consciousness or cranial-nerve changes to anxiety without neurological assessment may delay recognition of serious disease.
sections.clinicalPearl: Brainstem symptoms are often disproportionate to lesion size because many critical pathways are packed into a small space.
sections.practicalExample: A pontine lesion may combine ipsilateral facial weakness with contralateral limb weakness because a cranial-nerve nucleus and corticospinal tract are affected together.
sections.limitationsCautions: New diplopia, dysphagia, dysarthria, collapse, respiratory change or altered consciousness warrants urgent medical assessment.

anatomy.label: Midbrain
anatomy.function: Eye movements, orienting, motor modulation and arousal
anatomy.inputs: Cortical, retinal, cerebellar and sensory input
anatomy.outputs: Thalamic, spinal, cerebellar and cranial-motor outputs
anatomy.connections: Cortical, retinal, cerebellar and sensory input; projects via Thalamic, spinal, cerebellar and cranial-motor outputs.
anatomy.associatedDisorders: Oculomotor deficits, altered arousal, parkinsonian signs
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Assess midbrain in the context of lesion location, laterality, tract involvement and functional change.

anatomy.label: Pons
anatomy.function: Cortico-cerebellar relay, facial sensation and movement, sleep regulation
anatomy.inputs: Cortical, cerebellar, vestibular and sensory input
anatomy.connections: Cortical, cerebellar, vestibular and sensory input; projects via Cerebellar, cranial-motor and long-tract outputs.
anatomy.associatedDisorders: Facial weakness, gaze palsy, ataxia, locked-in syndrome
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Assess pons in the context of lesion location, laterality, tract involvement and functional change.

anatomy.label: Medulla
anatomy.function: Cardiorespiratory control, swallowing and lower cranial functions
anatomy.inputs: Visceral, spinal, vestibular and cortical input
anatomy.connections: Visceral, spinal, vestibular and cortical input; projects via Autonomic, cranial-motor and spinal outputs.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Assess medulla in the context of lesion location, laterality, tract involvement and functional change.

anatomy.label: Reticular formation
anatomy.function: Arousal, attention, sleep-wake regulation and pain modulation
anatomy.outputs: Thalamic, hypothalamic, cortical and spinal outputs
anatomy.connections: Diffuse sensory and cortical input; projects via Thalamic, hypothalamic, cortical and spinal outputs.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Assess reticular formation in the context of lesion location, laterality, tract involvement and functional change.

anatomy.label: Long tracts
anatomy.function: Carry motor, somatosensory and autonomic information through the brainstem
anatomy.inputs: Cortex, spinal cord and peripheral sensory systems
anatomy.outputs: Spinal cord, thalamus, cerebellum and cortex
anatomy.connections: Cortex, spinal cord and peripheral sensory systems; projects via Spinal cord, thalamus, cerebellum and cortex.
anatomy.associatedDisorders: Weakness, sensory loss, ataxia and crossed signs
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Assess long tracts in the context of lesion location, laterality, tract involvement and functional change.
